newsitem.title: UK: Derivatives markets wince at NatWest loss.
newsitem.headline: Derivatives markets wince at NatWest loss.

text.p: Derivatives markets are faced once again with the task of rebuilding investor confidence in the wake of National Westminster Bank's announcement that it will take a 50 million pounds ($81.14 million) charge for options pricing errors, traders said.

It comes at a time when the market is still recovering from the impact of the collapse of Barings in 1995 under the weight of 800 million pounds ($1.3 billion) of losses in unathorised derivatives trading.
"It's a complete pain," said a derivatives salesman at a major European bank in London. "We had a hard enough time after Barings in selling derivatives to clients."
"Now, every time we approach them, they are starting from the premise that we are a bunch of crooks," he said.
NatWest shocked the market late on Friday with the announcement of the loss provision for trades done in its investment banking arm, NatWest Markets.

Banking sources said former employee Kyriacos Papouis had been reported to the Securities and Futures Authority (SFA) and a senior trader, understood to be Neil Dodgson, had been suspended for failing to supervise his junior.
Papouis was not immediately available for comment and a spokeswoman for NatWest said it was conducting a thorough investigation into internal and external controls.
As details of the error remained sketchy, traders expressed surprise that mispricing, which occurred during 1996, had taken so long to surface.

Under guidelines issued by the Futures and Options Association (FOA) of which NatWest is a member, derivatives valuations should be checked and audited on a timely basis by an independent office, perhaps as often as daily.
"If I'd done this, the back office would have been on the phone the next day," said a senior derivatives trader at a major British bank in London.
Anthony Belchambers, chief executive of the FOA said the public and the private image of derivatives were markedly different.

"The problem is that when something goes wrong, the whole world knows," he said. "But the successful use of derivatives as a hedging tool is never seen because banks are unwilling, for commercial reasons to release that information."
Derivatives traders said talk in the market was that Papouis, who resigned from NatWest to take up a post with Bear Stearns last year, was betting heavily on a rise in British interest rates.

His trades, likely to have been swaps or swaptions, would have been over-the-counter (OTC), rather than traded on an exchange such as the London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE).
The senior British bank trader noted that it is possible to undertake much larger trades on an OTC basis, where the contract is made to measure between two counterparties.
A director of derivatives at a British securities house said around 70 percent of interest rate derivatives are traded on an OTC basis, bypassing the need for a clearing house.

"Inevitably this casts a shadow on all derivatives trading," said the derivatives director. "I'd like to see the FOA saying quite clearly that if banks are giving their traders this kind of license, it is doing the whole business no good at all."

Belchambers said the FOA had recently set up a working party to look at the issue of back office working practises, and from June would also be offering courses for compliance officers which covers risk management.
"Financial markets need derivatives and they are here to stay," said the senior British bank trader. "They may be the lesser of two evils, but they aren't going away."
